speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Following the end of the Second World War, the colonial era came to an end and a new world order was set up by the allies focused on global interdependence and cooperation amongst countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: International organisations, such as the UN, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, were set up in Bretton Woods to facilitate peace and security and to assist the world in transition.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As countries gained independence after the War, all countries, big and small, had a say in these organisations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Cold War never really erupted into a world war, I believe, in large part, because all major players respected international norms and laws.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a small country, we spoke up strongly against any violation of international norms, particularly in relation to the use of force, and also did our part to assist other countries grow and develop.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We made many friends on the international stage by looking for win-win outcomes with our counterparts, be it in trade or investments, and shared our own ideas freely with anyone interested.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These feelings have always been there, but what has been remarkable in 2016 is how strongly these have emerged in the political scene, particularly even countries, such as the US and UK, the two largest powers in the English-speaking world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In France, Europe's largest country, Marine Le Pen is campaigning on a platform that is anti-immigration and anti-EU.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If so, that may well mean the start of the end of the EU as we know it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Meanwhile, security challenges posed by organised terrorist groups and other lone wolf attacks continue to threaten society, given the transnational nature of terrorism and violent extremism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the battles in Iraq and Syria rage with the so-called Islamic State, fighters travelling to and from the region continue to pose a threat in countries far and wide, from Europe to Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Closer to home, significant geopolitical shifts are taking place with countries in the region anxiously watching for early signs from the Trump administration as to whether and how the US will stay actively involved and engaged and how it intends to interact with China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These developments could prompt countries to adjust their positions accordingly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Meanwhile, longstanding issues like territorial disputes and historical issues continue to be sources of tension in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At a time when it is even more imperative for regional organisations like ASEAN to stay united in order to navigate external pressures and regional dynamics, it appears that there remain difficult issues on which ASEAN would struggle to take a united position, such as, for example, matters relating to the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, what does MFA see as the major challenges facing Singapore in this environment?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: How should we position ourselves in these uncertain times?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Sino-US relationship is a key major power relationship for Singapore and the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore has historically been a good friend to both countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore has always been a good and reliable friend to the US in the region from the time of its Independence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: At this stage, President Trump's approach towards China and how China would respond remains unclear.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: On the one hand, it was reassuring that President Trump reportedly had a good telephone conversation with Chinese President Xi Jinping on 9 February 2017.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Other newly appointed leaders have also met or spoken to their Chinese counterparts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chinese Premier Li Keqiang said on 21 February 2017 that a US-China trade war would benefit nobody.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The US has also made other threats, such as the threat to revise the One-China policy that had guided diplomatic relations since the Nixon era.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The US approach to Asia also remains uncertain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: On the one hand, President Trump campaigned on the back of undoing US free trade agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: On the other hand, his Secretary Rex Tillerson has reaffirmed that the US will continue to be a major player in the region and even stated they would take steps to prevent China accessing illegally built structures in the South China Sea − a point which caused consternation in China but which seemed to suggest that the US still views its role in Asia as important.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, it was only half a year ago that the Prime Minister conducted a marathon of diplomatic visits to our closest partners in the region.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In three months, he travelled to Laos to meet with ASEAN leaders, and to the US, China, Japan, India and Australia to affirm longstanding ties.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Things were looking up for our relations with these key countries.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Our principled foreign policy position has emphasised the international rule of law, commitment to an open economy and freedom of navigation, mutual respect for each other's independence, and armed neutrality.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This seems to have earned us a good deal of legroom as a small, sovereign city state among large powers.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Some even commented that we are punching above our weight in the international arena to influence outcomes for the common good.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Much of our foreign policy achievements are clearly due to our hardworking diplomatic corps, members of whom have been building on the foundation established by our premier statesman, the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But it is also becoming apparent that the global order is changing and changing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Even as the Prime Minister continued his diplomatic marathon, when he was visiting Japan in September, a Chinese state-owned newspaper stoked public anger by accusing Singapore of taking sides against China.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, I am glad that the issue with the seizure of the Terrex vehicle by Hong Kong Customs was handled with great care by China and Singapore and has come to pass.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, the public expressions and discussions resulting from the event do point to some critical challenges to Singapore in this changing global order.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The critical challenges pertain to a rising China with the economic and military clout to impose its will on Asia.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: China may not do so in the near future, but with the means and its strong position on the South China Sea claims, the potential is there.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Whether we like it or not, China is an important strategic partner.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, even as Singapore invests in new opportunities of bilateral cooperation, especially under China's "Belt and Road" initiative, we need to be mindful of not becoming too dependent on the Chinese economy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have encouraged our businessmen, entrepreneurs and professionals to connect with their Chinese counterparts using deep historical and cultural links.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We saw the complications when Singaporeans doing business and working in China came under public pressure during the events last year.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Some Singaporeans were even of the opinion that we should appease China.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Singapore not only risks becoming economically vulnerable to any strategic foreign policy shift by China, the multiracial and multicultural character of our society will also come under pressure.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The US looks set to turn inwards to deal with domestic political conflicts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If the US disengages from Southeast Asia, this will leave a gap, if not a vacuum.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If ASEAN continues to be divided on the collective response to the South China Sea issue, then the gap left by the US will mean ASEAN will have to face a strong China by ourselves and divided.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, one of the tenets of our foreign policy is hard-nosed pragmatism to survive as a small city state.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Chairman, my next cut is on the outlook for Singapore-US relations.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Singapore has a long history of strong and close bilateral relationship with the US.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: We cooperate in many areas for mutual benefit.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Economic ties have been one of the cornerstones of our relationship with the US.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The Singapore-US FTA was implemented since 2004, one of the first FTAs signed by the US.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Many US companies have set up their regional headquarters here in Singapore, with a significant number of Americans living, working and studying here.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Similarly, many Singaporeans are drawn to study and work in the US.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The US has also been a firm supporter of maintaining regional peace and stability in Asia for many years, acting as a benign and constructive power.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This is an update to the 2005 Singapore-US DCA and also part of the bilateral Strategic Framework Agreement (SFA) between both sides.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The SFA underpins the close defence and security partnership that has contributed to maintaining regional peace and stability here in this region.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Chairman, all the above was prior to the US Presidential Elections in November last year.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Now, with the new Trump administration and its "America First" policy, I would like to ask the Minister how he sees Singapore-US relations evolving.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: He has also said that he wants to narrow the US trade deficits with countries, such as China, Germany, Japan, and may, indeed, adopt a protectionist posture with hefty import tariffs.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Fortunately for Singapore, the US actually has a trade surplus with us.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The question to the Minister is on the implications on Singapore which relies heavily on open and free trade.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Also, does the Minister see new opportunities for Singapore to be working even closer with the new US administration for mutual benefit?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Chairman, I move on to the next cut on Singapore-China relations and also Singapore's role as the coordinator for ASEAN-China Dialogue.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Relations between Singapore and China have been good for many years.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: More than 20 years ago, back in 1994, the China-Singapore Suzhou Industrial Park joint venture was formed.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This represented the first G-to-G economic cooperation project of its kind and on a scale not commonly seen.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This was followed by the Tianjin Eco-city Project in 2007 and, now, the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Singapore is one of China's largest foreign investors.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In fact, I think it is the largest foreign investor in China.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: To deepen economic cooperation further, a slew of projects was recently signed at the China-Singapore Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation meeting co-chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Teo Cee Hean and Chinese Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Beyond economic cooperation, Singapore-China relations are also complemented by collaboration between the Civil Service College here and China's Tsinghua University for the training and development of public policy leaders.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: People-to-people ties and cultural roots are also deep and strong.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Many Singaporeans also visit China for business and leisure.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Notwithstanding the strong and broad political, economic and social ties between the two countries, there would be occasional differences.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Ultimately, a prosperous and successful China which remains engaged in this region will augur well for the balance of power and, therefore, improve the stability for the region.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Singapore is also currently designated as the Coordinator for ASEAN-China dialogue.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: How can we play a constructive and useful role in bringing about better understanding and rapport between the two parties?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Would the Minister share with this House MFA's intended approach in this regard?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Wang Yi, the Chinese Foreign Minister, in a meeting with Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, said, "I hope both sides can work doubly hard through the actual actions of our cooperation to fully embody the characterisation of the bilateral relationship that we share, which is an all-round cooperative partnership, progressing with the times".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is our interpretation of what he had said and can MFA update us as to how Singapore can navigate the opportunities and challenges in this bilateral relationship?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Both countries have strong cultural, people-to-people, trade, finance and investment links.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's relations with our immediate neighbours, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia, remain of great importance to us.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: As close neighbours, developments in these countries invariably have an impact on us and it is crucial that we remain invested in building good relationships with them.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Many positive initiatives, such as the KL-Singapore High Speed Rail (HSR), the JB-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS), and joint property developments, such as Marina One and the DUO, were pursued in a spirit of good neighbourliness.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: These projects will bring our people closer together.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: To many Singaporeans, it would appear that bilateral relations have never been better.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: We believed that the issue of sovereignty over Pedra Branca had been closed by the ICJ's decision years ago.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Given these developments, I seek an assessment from the Minister for Foreign Affairs on our current relations with Malaysia and whether Malaysia's decision to apply for a revision of the ICJ judgment has affected the overall tenor of the relationship.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: I note that the Minister for Foreign Affairs recently hosted his Indonesian counterpart's visit to Singapore, and that Prime Minister Lee and President Jokowi held a Leaders' Retreat and opened an industrial park in Indonesia last year.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: What were some of the recent highlights and what is the Minister's assessment of Singapore's relationship with Indonesia?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: We have always described Singapore's relationship with Brunei as a "special relationship".

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: It is a longstanding and close relationship, the foundations of which were firmly laid by Brunei's late Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien and Singapore's founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Would the Minister be able to give us an update on the status of our bilateral relations and the trajectory of the relationship over the next few years?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Chairman, the ICJ's judgment in May 2008 had resolved a longstanding territorial dispute between Singapore and Malaysia in a peaceful and amicable manner.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Both sides had undertaken to respect and abide by the ICJ's judgment.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Then Malaysian Foreign Minister Rais Yatim had also described the outcome as a "win-win situation".

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on Singapore's response to Malaysia's application and whether this case will affect bilateral relations with Malaysia?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Will ongoing projects, such as the High Speed Rail, be affected?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The previous application to ICJ took about four years from submission to judgment.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How long does MFA expect this revision to take and what would the key milestones be?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore and Indonesia have enjoyed good relations for many years and share strong trade and cultural links, despite having some inevitable differences in various areas over the years.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore has been among the top three foreign investors in Indonesia and tourism between the two countries remains strong.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Furthermore, I would like to ask if there are plans for a Golden Jubilee celebration with Indonesia.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, how can ASEAN remain relevant in the future, in view of the changing geopolitical landscape?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Its main role is to promote regional peace and stability, accelerate economic growth, social progress and cultural development in the region, and also maintain close cooperation with international organisations with similar purposes.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Although ASEAN has been in existence for 50 years, not many people in the ASEAN countries understand the key roles and operations of ASEAN and how ASEAN has benefited them.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In fact, some have criticised ASEAN to be a talk-shop among political leaders without achieving any desirable outcomes that benefit its businesses and people.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some have said that ASEAN is "big on words but small on action", and ASEAN policies have proven to be mostly rhetoric, rather than actual implementation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In my opinion, ASEAN should focus on three areas.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: One, strengthen the unity among ASEAN countries so as to achieve peace and stability in the region.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Political leaders and government officials must put in more efforts to further improve diplomatic relations among countries and friendship among government officials.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Two, promote more partnerships among businesses in ASEAN countries to create better jobs for our people.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: More trade missions should be organised to facilitate business partnerships, investments and promotion of goods and services among ASEAN countries.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Three, encourage more people-to-people exchanges and interactions to foster stronger friendships among our people.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should encourage twin cities arrangements so that more opportunities can be created for residents of different ASEAN countries or cities to know each other better.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will further strengthen the unity of ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Relationships have been warm and constructive in the last few years, especially with neighbouring Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While we share some core common values and positions, the diverse political backgrounds and ever-changing circumstances within each country will inevitably lead to situations where we need to manage some of the differences and potential tension points that will surface from time to time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Maintaining strong and resilient political, economic and people-to-people ties within our region is, hence, very important in a region as diverse as Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is Singapore doing to maintain strong links with our fellow ASEAN countries?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we deepen Singaporeans' understanding of and familiarity with political developments in ASEAN, its culture and sensitivities and its economic opportunities?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are, indeed, good potential opportunities and sound commercial reasons for our companies to expand and internationalise into the region.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: What is the status of ASEAN integration, or has the South China Sea issue effectively blocked any progress for integration?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: If so, what are the implications for ASEAN unity, given the Philippines is the ASEAN Chair this year?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: This is not obvious to me as a lay person, as it seems that it is in China's interest to have a divided ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Historically, great powers will seek to divide and rule and advance their own interests in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I am not sure China will be an exception, given its own imperial history.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: China continues to expand its economic influence in mainland Southeast Asia and even with Malaysia, and will seek leverage with small states, such as Brunei and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We, of course, have our principled foreign policy and will never compromise our independence.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: However, are we in a position to help unite ASEAN and to block out any divisive forces?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: If we are not in that position, then are we able to facilitate processes or support another leading country, say, Indonesia, to help unite ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: If ASEAN is beginning to lose its viability, then what alternatives does Singapore have to try to achieve a semblance of stability in its surrounding waters?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, Japan and the Republic of Korea are two important regional partners for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We commemorated the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Singapore and Japan last year, and the 40th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Singapore and the Republic of Korea in 2015.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Both these relationships are fuelled by strong economic cooperation and people-to-people ties.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we look towards the next significant milestone in these relationships, how can Singapore further strengthen our cooperation with key partners, such as Japan and the Republic of Korea, and explore new areas for cooperation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, there have been many interactions at the various levels − government-to-government, business-to-business and people-to-people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, how have we expanded cooperation with India following the Strategic Partnership that was signed during Prime Minister Modi's visit to Singapore in November 2015?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore and Australia share an extremely strong bilateral relationship.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Australia is a popular destination for many Singaporeans on holiday.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Its universities are internationally renowned and highly regarded.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They are a top choice of many of our Singapore youths who seek to pursue a tertiary education overseas.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Singapore and Australia also share many bilateral and international platforms which allow for close government-to-government communication and cooperation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Separately, Australia is also a key strategic partner of Singapore in the region.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Australia participates actively in regional forums, such as the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) and the East Asia Summit (EAS).

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In 2015, Singapore and Australia celebrated 50 years of diplomatic relations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As a small state, Singapore has a vital interest in advocating for and maintaining a rules-based international order.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As an open economy with our key focus on free trade, Singapore's external environment plays an important role in ensuring our continued development and success.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: International rules bring greater predictability and, more crucially, form the basis for international cooperation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is a shift in the international geopolitical landscape.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The rise in the economic might of China has made some question the sustainability of the US as the world's pre-eminent superpower.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is, however, no consensus on how this will affect the international order.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Vital issues, such as terrorism, cyber threats, climate change and pandemics, present new perspectives on global challenges that have shifted the traditional paradigm of solutions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These are issues that are transboundary in nature and require the collective efforts of the entire international community as a whole in search of effective solutions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Closer to home, in the Asia Pacific region, countries are developing fast and growing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In time to come, the interests of these countries will come to the fore as their ability to defend their interests grows.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This will significantly change the geopolitical dynamics in the region.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: International Organisations, such as the UN, WTO, IMF, ICAO, IMO, G20 and APEC, are, therefore, critical multilateral platforms that will allow small states, such as Singapore, to engage the international community and contribute to possible solutions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These forums are vital platforms that can assist in the creation of global norms or rules in areas, such as international trade, finance, health and the environment.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is, therefore, imperative that Singapore continues to engage deeply and participate actively in such multilateral organisations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we fail to do so, our views will not be taken into account and this will be detrimental to our long-term strategic interests.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I invite the Minister to share with us on: (a) Singapore's position as a small state in the international order and multilateral system; and (b) how Singapore can help to strengthen the multilateral system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent months, unexpected electoral outcomes around the world have brought about unforeseen challenges.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a country that treasures not only our sovereignty but also our multiracial and multi-religious way of life, instances of pressure from major powers may raise anxiety among fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In such a situation, it is important for Singaporeans to understand why we need to remain steadfast by not bending to take sides and, more critically, why Singapore adheres to a principled position of upholding international rule of law, even though this may cause certain levels of unhappiness from some of our major partners.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As such, it is important for the Government to explain the considerations behind our foreign policy and to assure us that this is in Singapore's and Singaporeans' best interest.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How then can MFA better engage our public on Singapore's foreign policy and to explain the challenges Singapore faces from our external environment?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: First, in this rapidly changing and uncertain world, how does MFA review its work processes and allocate its resources to respond effectively in protecting the interests of Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Second, what sort of training programmes must MFA staff undergo in order to be operationally-ready?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: In today's ever-changing geopolitical situations and the high-speed flow of information, there is a need to develop new capabilities among our MFA staff to better respond to these challenges.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Smartphone applications and the Internet have allowed information and news, including fake news, to travel fast and reach out to many people which, in turn, affect political developments rapidly.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Thus, our MFA staff − especially those involved in overseas missions − must be tech-savvy to respond effectively in a dynamic political environment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, to say that the last financial year has been a public education in diplomacy for many younger Singaporeans would be an understatement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the issue appears to have been resolved and relations with China back on the usual even keel, some keen observers continue to watch the signature of Singapore's military activities in Taiwan, even as others viewed the episode as a shrewd diplomatic ploy by China to make a point about the One China Policy and to signal dissatisfaction with Singapore's position on the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Closer to home, it was significant that strategy number one of the seven strategies arising out of the Committee on the Future Economy was to deepen and diversify Singapore's international connections and to press ahead with trade and investment cooperation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of this renewed strategy cast against a broader evolutionary geopolitical environment, does the Ministry plan to review its staffing requirements, both locally and in overseas Embassies and High Commissions, with a view to raising manpower?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Chairman, recent global developments point towards increasingly inward-looking and protectionist sentiments in countries, such as the UK and the US.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The resulting uncertainty that pervades the region, coupled with the global economic slowdown, could have serious implications for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Recent leadership changes and upcoming elections in some of our neighbours would also have an impact on the current state and dynamics within our region.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Our trade figures are about two to three times our GDP.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Our immediate economic hinterland would be our Southeast Asian neighbours.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The region offers much potential and many opportunities for economic collaboration.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: In this context, I would like an update on the state of our economic relations with Southeast Asian countries and how has Singapore been strengthening our economic ties with our neighbours?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: How could and should our people and businesses contribute towards the relationship?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Chairman, Sir, UK's Brexit, with the complex and prolonged negotiations involved, continues to occupy the minds of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Aside from dampening economic growth, Brexit is a sign of inclination towards isolationism in the West.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As a small nation that depends heavily on foreign trade and diplomacy, increasing isolationism is a cause for concern.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Thanks to Government efforts, our ties with the EU have been cordial.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The EU actively engages with ASEAN in trade.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Among ASEAN nations, we are the EU's largest trading partner and also the 17th largest trading partner in the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Our nation has also been a major destination for European investments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: With the UK being one of the strongest economies and markets in Europe, Brexit would undoubtedly challenge our trade dynamics with the EU.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What will this mean for the European Union-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (EUSFTA), which has concluded negotiations, but has yet to be officially implemented?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Going forward, what is being done to continue to strengthen relations with Europe?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Moreover, on the economic and diplomatic front, how will we strengthen ties with an independent UK?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MINDEF also began humanitarian assistance disaster relief missions as far back as 1970.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government also frequently contributes cash donations via humanitarian organisations, such as the Red Cross and Mercy Relief.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have the capability and resources to do more to help our neighbours and I would urge us to do so on the grounds of compassion to strengthen bilateral ties and to strengthen stability and prosperity in our region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Chairman, the Singapore Cooperation Programme (SCP) is a series conducted by the Government to facilitate the sharing and empowerment with developing countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We share technical and systems skills and also human resources development which is seen as a vital and strategic move for economic and social progress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How efficient and effective have our efforts been in assisting these countries over the years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How does the Ministry monitor this and what are the KPIs set?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Whilst customisation may happen upon request from receiving countries, how frequently do we review our programmes and ensure relevance and applicability?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One more observation is that the SCP programmes may not just be executed by Singapore alone but in partnerships, for example, the Singapore-Canada Third Country Training Programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In such cases, how big is our voice, our partnership and also contribution, and how are these decided upon in the sharing and cooperation?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It charts out 17 Sustainable Development Goals that provide a framework for countries to address global issues, such as poverty, gender equality, climate change and sustainable development, among others.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While the Goals are aspirational in nature and not legally binding, achieving these goals is no small feat and will require all countries to work together, including Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As a small country with limited land and resources, we understand first-hand both the imperative and the challenges of sustainable development.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What we are able to achieve on our own is limited in the grand scheme of things, as the outcome of global climate change will hinge on decisions taken by all countries, especially the major economies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Nonetheless, as an active and responsible member of the international community, it is important that we play a constructive role to help forge a global consensus and to contribute in small but meaningful ways.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In this regard, how is Singapore cooperating with other countries and international agencies to tackle global issues, such as sustainable development and climate change?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are entering a more challenging economic environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Growth in the developed markets has become more subdued.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are growing protectionist sentiments in some countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a small and open economy with foreign trade more than three times our GDP, Singapore is particularly vulnerable to economic shifts and, more worryingly, protectionist measures.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As articulated in the recently released Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) Report, one of the strategies to take Singapore forward in this challenging global climate is to "deepen and diversify our international connections".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Indeed, beyond traditional markets like Southeast Asia and China, emerging markets, such as South Asia, Africa, Latin America and Central Asia, offer growth potential and pockets of opportunities for our businesses abroad.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore should take the opportunity to strengthen our partnership with these countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In view of this, I would like to ask what MFA is doing to expand our linkages with the emerging markets, including political and people-to-people linkages.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This region is also home to several major and promising economies, such as Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, all of whom are in the G20, along with the Pacific Alliance, a regional trade bloc comprising Chile, Colombia, Peru and Mexico.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This was also the first visit by President Tan to the Latin American region.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: What further steps, therefore, is the Ministry taking to broaden and deepen our commitment to these bilateral ties, to expand political, economic, educational, cultural and also people-to-people links?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The political and security situation in the Middle Eastern countries continues to be uncertain and in a state of flux.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The wars in Syria and Yemen are still ongoing.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Israeli-Palestinian issue has not made any progress.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As major oil producers, countries in the Middle East have been impacted by the low oil prices.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Can the Minister provide an update on Singapore's engagement with the Middle East?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Besides economic engagement, what the other areas are we working on with the Middle Eastern countries?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Chairman, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict is a deeply complex issue that has confronted the Middle East for decades.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The international community has tried to assist in resolving the question but with limited success.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It is an emotive and complex issue, not only in the Middle East, but also here in Singapore and the Southeast Asia region.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Despite the difficulties, it is important to find a solution, one that can help achieve a just and durable peace, with Israelis and Palestinians living side-by-side in security.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It is clear that there is no straight-forward solution to this longstanding conflict.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Building trust and confidence between parties is the key building block towards a solution.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Singapore, on our part, has friendly ties with both Israel and the Palestinian National Authority.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Earlier in April 2016, Prime Minister Lee had visited Israel, the Palestinian Territories and Jordan.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Mr Hawazi has since made his first visit, as Singapore's Representative, to the West Bank in January 2017.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I invite the Minister to share with us on: the impact of international conferences, such as the Conference for Peace in the Middles held in Paris earlier this year; Singapore's position on the issue and the reasons behind it; and any updates and outcomes of Senior Minister of State Dr Maliki Osman and Mr Hawazi Daipi's working visits to the Palestinian Territories.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Singapore is one of the smallest nations of the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Many, however, have described us as "punching well above our weight" in terms of economic, political, foreign policies and security relevance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Making friends and influencing others require us to be tactful and move with the highest level of diplomacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Our location at the crossroads of the west and the east, and the north and south also plays a strategic role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: But that leaves us open to a variety of potential threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We keep cordial relations with other nations and, especially our regional neighbours and partners, and, at the same time, we have to look after our own interests and existence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: With the current challenges the world is facing, how are we positioning and preparing ourselves and consistently maintaining high alert on the "goings on"?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Are we reviewing our bilateral, multilateral, regional and global relationships and contributions?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More Singaporeans are also living and working abroad these days.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Notwithstanding these operational challenges, I wish to commend our MFA officers for their professionalism and dedication in working around the clock, especially during crises and emergencies, to provide the necessary support to affected Singaporeans and their families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is thanks to their hard work that many Singaporeans are able to travel overseas with the necessary assurances and peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How are MFA officers equipping themselves to ensure that Singaporeans continue to receive quality consular services?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does MFA facilitate the transmission of experience from older and retired MFA staff to their younger colleagues?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there room for retired MFA staff and Singaporeans living overseas to assist or contribute to our Missions in their operations on a volunteer basis?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also, what travel advice should Singaporeans take note of, especially those who travel frequently?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Twenty sixteen was a tumultuous year for the world and a very busy year for MFA staff.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The previous global consensus on the benefits of free trade and economic integration is broken.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Unfortunately, unlike in this House, political discourse in many countries has become increasingly nationalistic, anti-incumbent and, even sometimes, xenophobic.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The threat from terrorism, radicalisation and extremism has increased and new media has also amplified this threat far and wide.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Quite frankly, we have to anticipate even more of such external challenges and challenges that will test our resolve, unity and agility.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As a small city state, Singapore has no option.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Isolation and protectionism are not an option for us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, the world is even more interconnected than ever before.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We actually have to double down on globalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, for us, free trade is not a debating point.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If you think about it, the larger context of this Budget debate, of the Committee of Supply (COS) and of the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) is that we have to enhance the competitive position of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That is the only way we can survive and thrive in this uncertain world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Add to that the fact that major power interactions and rivalry will impact our region and will impact us, and we have seen evidence of that.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The question, therefore, that all Members have posed is: how will we navigate these challenges?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are still a tiny island in an uncertain neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We still have to try our best to build a network of friends.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have to be a relevant, valuable and reliable partner and, at the same time, be realistic about our place in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As the former British Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary Lord Palmerston once pointed out, nations have no permanent friends or allies; they only have permanent interests.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our key foreign policy principles, therefore, have not changed.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First, we conduct an independent sovereign foreign policy in order to safeguard our independence and the interests of all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And third, we have to remain committed to a rules-based international system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And one point which I want to commend today − I have listened to the very thoughtful speeches from Mr Low Thia Khiang, Mr Pritam Singh − and I am grateful for the bipartisan support that we have in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This unity of purpose is essential for us to pursue our foreign policy goals in this uncertain and volatile environment.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: All Members of this House understand and appreciate the key tenets of our policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Many Members have asked questions about Singapore's long-term value proposition and the relevance of Singapore to other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ms Sun Xueling asked about Singapore-China relations; Mr Cedric Foo asked about the US-Singapore relations under the new Trump administration; Mr Amrin Amin and Dr Chia Shi-Lu have asked for updates on our relations with Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore has been a steadfast and long-standing friend of China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our bilateral relationship right now, I would describe it as in "good working order".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Put aside the words, the point is, historically, our relationship has been built on the strong foundations laid by Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Mr Deng Xiaoping.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And over the decades, Singapore has supported, and demonstrated in action and investment, China's peaceful development and its progressive engagement of the regional and international community.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Several Cabinet Members, including myself, had just accompanied Deputy Prime Minister Teo to Beijing.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We attended the Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation (JCBC).

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It was a very good meeting and it gave both sides opportunities to explore ways to deepen cooperation especially in this flagship project of President Xi Jinping, the Belt and Road initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I also had a very good meeting with my counterpart, and I can say that this, again, is a reflection of the deep resilient nature of our relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Besides the JCBC, we also have candid exchanges and sharing of experiences through established platforms, such as the China-Singapore Forum on Leadership and the Singapore-China Social Governance Forum.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The various projects, the business engagements, the people-to-people ties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: You have heard: 2.8 million Chinese tourists come to Singapore and I think, for us, it would be 800,000 Singaporeans who have travelled to China in a year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The high frequency of interactions at senior leadership level has conferred a very high degree of resilience and, I would add, strategic trust, in our relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, even when we have differences over some issues, as I have said in an earlier session, we should not overact and we should, in a sense, anticipate that these incidents are not unusual even amongst close friends and neighbours, and we must recognise that our shared interests far exceed these differences.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must not be distracted from the larger strategic imperatives or allow incidents to derail the substantive, longstanding and mutually-beneficial cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo will elaborate on the more specific details of our relationship with China, as well as give you an update on the JCBC after this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There is a new administration; it is settling in.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There is always a period of uncertainty, a period of adjustment that goes on both domestically and also at the international level when a new administration takes over, basically because the US is such an important superpower.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As far as Singapore is concerned, we believe that our many decades of consistent policies and interactions with the US have created trust and I believe they consider us a reliable partner.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I am confident that we will be creative and adaptable in developing win-win partnerships with the US even as President Trump pursues a new set of policies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have had a strong and enduring base of relations for the last 51 years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These mutually-beneficial ties have spanned five Republican and four Democratic administrations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On the defence front, our Air Force has training detachments in Texas, Idaho and Arizona.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US is a significant user of both Changi Naval Base and Paya Lebar Air Base.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And Singapore also supports the rotational deployment of the US Littoral Combat Ships and the P8 Poseidon aircraft.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These fundamentals of our relationship remain unchanged and their value is recognised by both Republican and Democratic administrations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Similarly, the strategic and economic imperatives that have underpinned America's longstanding engagement of our region actually remain unchanged.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have to constantly look for new areas of convergence for win-win cooperation with the US.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For instance, one of the more recent things we are working on is on cybersecurity and we signed an MOU on Cybersecurity Cooperation in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Low Thia Khiang also asked some searching questions about how the relationship between China and the US will impact Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Indeed, this is the key bilateral relationship that will affect peace, security and prosperity in our region and, indeed, the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Whilst competition between the US and China is inevitable, but what is different in historical terms is that never before have two powers been so interdependent, so intertwined economically.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Even in the depths of the Cold War, remember that the American and Russian economies were never intertwined to the same degree that the US and Chinese economies are.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, we hope that both sides, after they have measured these imperatives, will come back to the same conclusion that constructive engagement and win-win cooperation are the right formula.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If they can achieve this, this will provide space for countries in the region, including Singapore, to be part of a common circle of friends and achieve win-win outcomes for all.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is, in fact, a key reason why for the last 51 years, Southeast Asia, in particular, the founding members of ASEAN, have enjoyed peace, security, prosperity over the last five decades.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We hope that they will arrive at this conclusion.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But we should also bear in mind that we have no say.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We cannot determine the dynamics of that relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Low asked: what do we do if they do not get along?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And the answer is that, number one, we have no say; number two, we should avoid being forced to choose sides for as long as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The third point is that we must always remain an honest broker.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: What that means is, whatever I tell the Secretary of State of the US, I must also be prepared to take the same consistent position with the Foreign Minister of China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I do not say two different things and hope that they never compare notes.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have to be clear, consistent and transparent in our communications.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The other point is to try to do as much as possible on a bilateral basis with both China and the US and, if possible, in third-party projects in other parts of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Again, it is a matter of maintaining strategic consistency while having tactical agility.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I do not want to trivialise it and say that this will be very easy − it will not be – but watch this space, we will come back to you and update you as things progress, and I hope that all Members of the House, including the Opposition, will continue to support MFA.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Closer to home, our relationship with Malaysia is actually as good as it ever has been.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is a landmark agreement that will transform the way both countries interact and do business.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It will bring our two peoples and economies even closer together.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The RTS will improve the flow of people and business between Singapore and Johor and bring both sides closer together.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On the whole, our bilateral relations are excellent.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Other than these connectivity initiatives, the economic and people-to-people ties remain strong.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will continue to cooperate on security, defence and counter-terrorism.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng and others asked about the Pedra Branca case and how this impacts our bilateral relations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Part of what underpins our good relations with Malaysia is a commitment by both sides to resolve disagreements amicably in accordance with international law while allowing mutually-beneficial cooperation to continue in the meantime.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, you will recall that in 2003, Singapore and Malaysia agreed to submit the case concerning sovereignty over Pedra Branca, Middle Rocks and South Ledge to the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Under Article 61, an application for revision of a judgment must satisfy several criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These criteria include that it must be based upon the discovery of facts which were unknown to the court and to the party claiming revision when judgment was first given; and these newly-discovered facts must be decisive and of such a character as to lay the case open to revision.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: An application for revision must also be made, at the latest, within six months of the discovery of the new fact and within 10 years of when the judgment was given.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our legal team has studied Malaysia's application carefully, including the three documents relied on by Malaysia to support its application.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are confident of our legal team and our case.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are very fortunate to still have Prof Jayakumar, Senior Judge Chan Sek Keong and Ambassador-at-Large Tommy Koh who led our original Pedra Branca team.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They are also working very hard now, very enthusiastically, I may add.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They are also working with a younger team of bright legal minds in the AGC.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This way, we are also using this episode as an opportunity to build up expertise and experience in the next generation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is important as I am sure there will be more international legal issues in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Equally, we must ensure that the same whole-of-Government spirit of unity prevails.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These are crucial ingredients in order for Singapore to punch above our weight at international fora.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore is committed to resolving this issue amicably and in accordance with international law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Bilateral relations with Malaysia, therefore, are good, will remain good, and we will continue with all our mutually beneficial bilateral programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singaporeans should not be disconcerted by these developments because, even with the best of diplomatic and personal relationships, we must expect other states to act in their own self-interests.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong and President Joko Widodo had a successful Leaders' Retreat in Semarang last November.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They jointly witnessed the opening of the Kendal Industrial Park, and agreed to set up an Indonesia-Singapore Business Council and to explore cooperation in both the energy and tourism sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The positive and stable relationship that we have enjoyed in recent times has been mutually beneficial.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore remains Indonesia's top foreign investor in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This year, we celebrate 50 years of diplomatic relations with Indonesia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This was a demonstration of how both countries can work together to resolve bilateral issues in areas of mutual interest, in accordance with international law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is an important principle that both sides share because, as neighbours, we must expect disagreements to arise from time to time, but what matters is how we resolve these disagreements.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore and Brunei, of course, share a longstanding and a special relationship, anchored in deep mutual trust and respect, which have been built up over decades, over generations of leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is epitomised by the Currency Interchangeability Agreement, which marks its 50th anniversary this year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will continue to build on this special relationship with the younger generation of Bruneian leaders though platforms like the Singapore-Brunei Young Leaders Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: More broadly, Southeast Asia is our immediate hinterland.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And as many Members have said, ASEAN serves a crucial role as the main platform for regional cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: ASEAN has kept our region peaceful and allowed Member States to focus on growing our economies and improving the lives of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Low Thia Khiang asked very timely and important questions about ASEAN's relevance, the pace of integration, the future of ASEAN unity and the key achievements as we celebrate its 50th anniversary.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Cedric Foo and others also asked about our coordinatorship of ASEAN-China Dialogue Relations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: ASEAN enables us to more effectively shape our external environment and to have our views taken into account by bigger players.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have a demographic dividend that is not yet harvested.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To maintain our relevance, ASEAN must continue to be neutral, to be united and to be committed to an open and inclusive regional architecture, and that means we have to continue to consolidate and deepen our economic integration.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We adopted the ASEAN Community Vision 2025 and the three Community Blueprints in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must do more to help Singaporeans better understand and identify with ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must also explore ways for ASEAN to ride the technological wave of the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will continue to partner with organisations like the Singapore Business Federation and the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises to help our businesses maximise the economic opportunities ASEAN presents.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will also work closely with the Philippines to ensure the success of its Chairmanship this year, and to begin preparations for our own ASEAN Chairmanship in 2018.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is important that we strive for an integrated, outward-looking and confident ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To that end, we hope to build new links with other regional organisations, for instance, the Pacific Alliance and the Eurasian Economic Union.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At the same time, the events unfolding in the EU are also a salutary reminder for us not to reprise their problems, and ASEAN must remain pragmatic and practical in managing the pace and the scale of the implementation of our economic integration.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The sequence, the pace and the scale − the implementation of all of these are very important.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: ASEAN's cohesion and unity, to be frank with you, have been tested by difficult issues, not only just last year but many times before.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Nonetheless, we have endured and we have even thrived over the past five decades.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Looking ahead, ASEAN will become more, not less, critical to our foreign policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I totally support Dr Teo Ho Pin's three suggestions on strengthening unity, promoting partnerships between businesses and encouraging more people-to-people ties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Now let me turn to our role as the Dialogue Relations coordinator between ASEAN and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Again, I want to stress that we have to be honest brokers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have to do our best to manage this strategic partnership based on mutual benefit and respect.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Relations with other countries − Japan, India, Australia and the EU − are also important, and I am glad to report that relations are also good and will deepen.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We commemorated 50 years of diplomatic relations with Japan in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We had a series of high-level exchanges, including a State Visit by President Tony Tan.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are working towards upgrading the Japan-Singapore Economic Partnership Agreement and our Air Services Agreement, and we hope to strengthen bilateral cooperation in air, land and sea transport and infrastructure through the inaugural Vice-Ministerial Transport Forum this year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In India, steady progress has been made under the Strategic Partnership signed when Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited us in November 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Strategic Partnership has allowed us to broaden and deepen relations in diverse areas, both at the centre as well as in selected states in India.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This was reaffirmed during Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong's visit to India in October 2016, when he launched the Centre of Excellence for Tourism Training (CETT) in Udaipur.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The master-planning of Andhra Pradesh's new capital city, Amaravati, by Singapore experts has been completed, and a Singapore consortium is now bidding to participate in the "seed development" of this brand new city.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore has a close and longstanding bilateral relationship with Australia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This was elevated in June 2015 with the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (CSP), and this is a substantive undertaking with over 40 bilateral initiatives that will be delivered through the period to 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have moved quickly to implement the CSP.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Key agreements were signed during the Prime Minister's visit to Australia in October 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Areas which, I may add, are multiples the size of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This will add significantly towards addressing the SAF's evolving training requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The upgrade to the Singapore-Australia FTA is expected to come into force this year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It will create many more opportunities for Singapore businesses and professionals to access the Australian markets.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are also working on the EU-ASEAN Comprehensive Air Transport Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore will also continue to seek economic links and opportunities for our companies in emerging markets, such as Africa, Latin America and the Middle East.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Senior Minister of State Dr Maliki will elaborate on this, after I have finished my contribution.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are one of the few countries that engage in a principled way with all the protagonists in the Middle East.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the short one and a half years that I have been here, I have accompanied the Prime Minister to Jordan, Israel and Ramallah, under the Palestine National Authority (PNA).

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have gone to the Temple Mount, visited the Dome of the Rock, Al-Aqsa Mosque, Church of the Holy Sepulchre, been welcomed by all parties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is amazing, if you think about it: us, tiny little Singapore, is welcomed by all parties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I believe we have this special position because we take a principled position.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we also work in a win-win way to support all parties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For instance, with the Palestinians, we have extended our technical assistance with the PNA.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But more importantly, I think, one of the key secret ingredients is the fact that Singapore itself is a successful model of multiracial, multi-religious integration.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because that gives us a special moral standing to be able to engage, speak and interact with all parties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Very few countries have this special role that we have.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Apart from all these engagements, bilateral and regional, we need to continue to support international economic groupings and arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Prime Minister Lee attended the G20 Summit in China last year at President Xi's invitation, and he will attend the G20 Summit in Hamburg in July this year at German Chancellor Angela Merkel's invitation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This will be the seventh time that Singapore is invited to attend a G20 Summit.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The next aspect that I want to talk about is how we pursue an independent foreign policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This means having a foreign policy that serves Singapore's and Singaporeans' interests, first and foremost.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin spoke about the importance of a rules-based international system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this is critical for a small state like Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: He asked how we can strengthen the multilateral system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As a small country, the rule of law is crucial for our survival.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
